visits.text: Nearly eight centuries: that is the age of the Great Mosque of Ajloun, one of the oldest still standing in Jordan. It dates to 1247, under the Ayyubids, Saladin’s dynasty. Its minaret was added in 1262 under the Mamluks, the sultans who succeeded them. The building was renovated in 2014. Stop for 15 minutes as you pass through the center before heading up to the castle.

Ajloun Castle (Qal'at ar-Rabad) is worth visiting above all for its location: its towers offer sweeping views over the northern Jordan Valley. Izz al-Din Usama, one of Saladin’s generals, made it a fortress in 1184. It was intended to protect the region’s iron mines. It also faced Belvoir Castle, held by the Crusaders, Christian knights from Europe. The Mongols damaged it in 1260, and earthquakes in 1837 and 1927 later hit it hard. A small museum displays Roman glassware and oil lamps.

“Elijah the Tishbite”: this is how the Bible names the prophet Elijah. Tradition places his hometown, Tishbe, in the ruins of Listib, just across a small valley facing Tell Mar Elias. This tell, a mound formed by centuries of settlement, holds the remains of two Byzantine churches, one dating to the 4th–5th centuries and the other to the 6th. A mosaic inscription there mentions the prophet. Come early in the morning before heading to the forest reserve.

activities.text: Next, take a round-trip cable car ride from the station near Ajloun Castle. Opened in 2023, the Ajloun cable car covers 2.5 km in about 10 minutes. It connects a station near the castle to Ishtafeina Forest. From the cabin, you look down over wooded hills and the fortress from above. In winter 2024, the last departures were around 4:30 p.m.: check the schedule before boarding.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Jordan in 5 Days: Jerash, Ajloun, Umm Qais

activities.text: Beneath the holm oaks, you can hear jays, tits, and finches. Ajloun Forest Reserve protects 13 km² of wooded hills, where carob and strawberry trees also grow. The Rasoun Trail (2 to 3 hours, with a local guide) climbs to the Eagle Viewpoint at around 1,100 m. It then descends toward the village of Rasoun and its Soap House, where women make olive oil soap. Short on time? The Roe Deer Trail covers 2 km and takes about 1 hour.

If you have never held a reed pen, a writing tool cut from reed or bamboo, now is your chance. At the House of Calligraphy, on the edge of Ajloun Forest Reserve, local women trained in Amman introduce the Arabic alphabet. You will then write your first letters in black ink. In the same area, the Biscuit House makes cookies and cereal bars without additives, which you can sample at the on-site café.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Jordan in 5 Days: Jerash, Ajloun, Umm Qais

visits.text: Allow for a day trip from Amman to visit Jerash. Jerash welcomes you through Hadrian's Arch, erected in 129 for the emperor's visit—a gateway measuring 25 m by 21 m leading into one of the best-preserved Roman cities in the Near East, sometimes nicknamed the “Pompeii of the East”. Pass the hippodrome, then emerge onto the Oval Plaza, a forum measuring 90 m by 80 m and the only oval-shaped one. Its first-century Ionic colonnade encloses a space used both as a market and a gathering place. The Cardo Maximus starts here, stretching 800 meters and lined with 200 Corinthian columns—you can still see the ruts left by chariots in the paving stones. Allow 2 to 3 hours for the site and bring a hat, as there is hardly any shade.

Don't leave Jerash without pushing on to the Temple of Artemis, dedicated to the city's patron goddess. Its 12-meter Corinthian columns still rise against the sky. The South Theater, built around 90 under Domitian, seated 5,000 spectators—climb to the upper tiers and test the acoustics by clapping your hands at the center of the stage. It still serves as a performance venue during the Jerash Festival in July.

Back in Amman (~1 hour's drive), climb to the Citadel on Jebel al-Qala'a hill at an elevation of 850 meters. The Temple of Hercules, commissioned under Marcus Aurelius between 162 and 166, preserves two 10-meter columns and three stone fingers from a colossal statue—the scale becomes dizzying when you imagine the original size. Just behind it, the Umayyad Palace, built around 720 and destroyed by the earthquake of 749, has a vaulted audience hall designed to impress the governor's visitors. Go in the late afternoon: at sunset, the panorama of Amman's thousands of beige houses and the Roman theater below is the best in the city.

Walk back down to the Roman Theater, carved into the rock in the 2nd century and able to seat 6,000 spectators. From there, plunge into the Downtown souk: the lively streets connect the theater to the al-Husseini Mosque. It's the perfect spot to taste your first mansaf (lamb stew in fermented yogurt, Jordan's national dish) or a hot falafel fresh from the fryer.
Enjoy one last morning snorkeling session on the reefs south of Aqaba—King Abdullah Reef has corals in excellent condition and hawksbill turtles.

Take the road back to Amman via the Dead Sea Highway, which follows the Jordan Valley (~4 hours' driving). The road itself is a spectacle: the cliffs of Wadi Araba on the left, the desert on the right, then the bluish surface of the Dead Sea appearing below.

Before heading to the airport, devote 2 hours to the Jordan Museum in the Ras al-Ain quarter. It's the country's largest museum (10,000 m²), with collections spanning prehistory to the present. The highlights: fragments of the Dead Sea Scrolls, discovered in the Qumran caves between 1947 and 1956—including the famous Copper Scroll that describes a hidden treasure—and the Ain Ghazal statues, 9,000 years old, among the world's oldest human statues.

If time permits, take a final stroll through Jabal al-Weibdeh, right next to the museum. The Darat al Funun gallery occupies several restored traditional houses overlooking downtown, with contemporary Arab art exhibitions and pleasant gardens. Entry is free.

activities.text: Evening stroll through the Rainbow Street quarter—cafés, art galleries and terraces with views over the lower city. On summer Fridays, the Souk Jara market sets up here with local crafts and street food.

Final evening in Amman—the Jabal al-Weibdeh quarter, with its art galleries, literary cafés and restaurants in buildings from the 1930s–1950s, offers an atmosphere very different from the historic center. Perfect for a quiet dinner and an after-dinner stroll.

visits.text: Arrival in Aqaba, Jordan's only coastal city, situated at the country's extreme south on the Gulf of Aqaba. Don't expect a paradise beach downtown—the charm lies underwater. Start with the seafront (Corniche) and the Mamluk fort, built in the 14th century and reinforced by the Ottomans, which controlled the trade routes between Asia and Africa.

Head toward South Beach, 10 km south of downtown, at the heart of Aqaba Marine Park, which stretches along 7 km of coastline. With a mask and snorkel, you can reach a coral reef directly from shore—no boat needed. Here, the Red Sea is home to over 200 species of coral and more than 1,000 fish species: clownfish in their anemones, yellow-tailed surgeonfish, lionfish and moray eels. A few meters from shore, you can spot an M42 military tank deliberately submerged at a depth of 6 meters to create an artificial reef.

Continue 5 minutes north of South Beach to the Japanese Garden, considered by many to be the best snorkeling spot in Jordan. Its hard and soft corals with rounded shapes recall a Japanese garden. The depth doesn't exceed 12 meters and visibility often reaches 30 to 40 meters.

activities.text: Grilled fish dinner on Aqaba's seafront—souk or Corniche restaurants serve fresh Red Sea fish, accompanied by hummus and warm bread.

days_plan.itin_title: Jordan Road Trip: Petra, Wadi Rum & the Dead Sea

visits.text: By the middle of the 20th century, Dana had lost almost all its residents. Yet this village of Ottoman-era stone houses had been inhabited for about 500 years. In the early 1990s, the RSCN, Jordan’s Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature, restored 65 houses and brought in water and electricity. The village overlooks Wadi Dana. The reserve descends from an elevation of 1,500 m to below sea level. Admission to the reserve costs 10 JD, plus taxes.

activities.text: Book Dana’s Village Tour through the RSCN at least 24 hours in advance. This walk of about 2 km takes two hours and climbs to the village springs. These three springs irrigate terraced gardens clinging to the slope. Along the way, workshops let you see women from the village making silver jewelry and preparing dried fruit. Their products are sold at the RSCN nature shop, alongside herbs and fabrics.

If you are traveling between March 15 and October 31, get up early for the Rummana Trail. From Dana, plan on a round trip by road to the Rummana access point, then continue to the campsite on foot or by the reserve’s shuttle. This 2.5 km trail starts at the campsite and takes two hours to walk, without a guide. It climbs to the summit of Jabal Rummana (jabal means mountain), across Wadi Dana, a few kilometers from the village. From the top, you look down over Wadi Araba, the long desert valley linking the Dead Sea to the Red Sea. Early in the morning, the nearby bird hide is the best place to watch for birds and Nubian ibex.

days_plan.itin_title: The King’s Highway in 6 Days: Madaba, Kerak, Dana, and Petra

visits.text: Start the day at Mount Nebo, 8 km from Madaba; allow for a day trip from your accommodation on the Dead Sea. This promontory at an altitude of 817 m is where, according to Deuteronomy, Moses contemplated the Promised Land before dying at the age of 120. On a clear day, you will see the Dead Sea, the Jordan Valley and sometimes Jerusalem in the distance. In front of the restored basilica (fourth-century foundations, rebuilt in 597), admire the Brazen Serpent, a bronze sculpture by Gian Paolo Fantoni combining Christ's cross and Moses' serpent. Inside, mosaics dated to 530 show hunting and grape-harvesting scenes on a panel measuring 9 m by 3.

Allow for a day trip from your accommodation on the Dead Sea to visit Madaba. Open the door of Saint George's Church in Madaba, a modest Orthodox building erected in 1896 over the ruins of a sixth-century Byzantine basilica. It houses the Madaba Map, the oldest cartographic representation of the Holy Land—more than 2 million stone tesserae assembled around 550–560, originally measuring 21 m by 7 m (16 m by 5 remain). You will recognize Jerusalem in the center, the Dead Sea with two boats, and the Jordan with its fish. Arrive early in the morning—tour groups quickly crowd this small church.

Stay in Madaba for the archaeological park, a few streets from Saint George's; visit it as part of a day trip from your accommodation on the Dead Sea. You will see other Byzantine mosaics, including those of the Hippolytus Hall and the Church of the Virgin. Madaba is nicknamed the “city of mosaics” - if the subject fascinates you, you can join an introductory workshop at one of the craft studios that keep the tradition alive.

Late in the day, descend toward the Dead Sea—the lowest point on the planet, roughly 430 meters below sea level. The water contains nearly 30% salt (versus 3–4% in the oceans), making floating inevitable. Coat yourself with the black mud rich in magnesium and potassium, let it dry for 20 minutes, then rinse in the salty water. Don't exceed 20 minutes of bathing per session, and above all never put your head underwater. Bring water shoes because the salt crystals on the bottom are sharp.

activities.text: Sunset from the shores of the Dead Sea—the low-angle light on the calm waters and the mountains of the West Bank opposite. Bring a book for the classic souvenir photo: reading while floating.

days_plan.itin_title: Jordan Road Trip: Petra, Wadi Rum & the Dead Sea

activities.text: The final 8 kilometers to Feynan are unpaved. Leave your car at the visitor center on the outskirts of Qurayqira village, pronounced “Greigra,” in a covered parking lot guarded day and night. A Bedouin driver then takes you up the track in a 4x4, a journey of about half an hour. The transfer costs 14.50 JD per vehicle for up to four people, added to your bill. Book it in advance; otherwise, expect a wait of 30 to 45 minutes.

Feynan’s most memorable outing takes you to the ancient copper mines. Copper was already being extracted here 6,500 years ago, in simple furnaces where the wind fanned the fire. Under the Romans, these became the largest copper mines in the Empire. In the 3rd and 4th centuries, prisoners, many of them Christians, were sent here to work until they died. With a Bedouin guide, you explore 4,000-year-old mine shafts. The ruins of Khirbet Feynan (khirbet means ruin) are those of the town where the mine administrators lived.

Climb the hills around Feynan late in the day on the sunset hike, included in your stay. Wadi Feynan opens out at the foot of the Great Rift’s escarpments. This rift is the long fracture in the Earth’s crust that formed the Jordan River valley and the Dead Sea. From the heights, you can see the land drop away toward Wadi Araba. Bring a headlamp for the return trip: night falls quickly, and the ecolodge is lit only by candles.

After dark, only handmade candles light the rooms at the Wadi Feynan ecolodge. Solar panels supply power only to reception, the bathrooms, and the kitchen. The rooms have no electrical outlets: charge your phone and camera at reception. With no lights nearby, the sky is ideal for stargazing, an outing included in your stay. In July and August, when it gets too hot, you can sleep on the rooftop terrace.

Neither a museum nor a show: in Wadi Feynan, neighboring Bedouin families welcome you, and many of their members work at the ecolodge. It was built in 2005 to give residents an alternative source of income to copper mining, which is no longer profitable. Sign up at reception to visit a Bedouin family or attend a cooking demonstration. These activities depend on the day’s program.

days_plan.itin_title: The King’s Highway in 6 Days: Madaba, Kerak, Dana, and Petra

visits.text: It is best to start exploring Jerash from the south, beneath Hadrian’s Arch. This triple-arched gateway was built in 129–130 for the visit of the Roman emperor Hadrian. Restored to its original height of 21 m, it stands as tall as a seven-story building. Just behind it stretches the hippodrome, a chariot-racing track and one of the smallest in the Roman world. The site opens at 8 a.m.: arrive early, before the heat and the groups.

Stop at the Jerash visitor center before entering the ancient city. A scale model, a short film, and information panels explain the city’s layout. Restored statues of Zeus and Aphrodite are on display. You can also hire a local guide here, useful for locating the churches. The ticket includes the archaeological museum. The Jordan Pass, a sightseeing pass that also includes the tourist visa fee, covers admission.

An oval plaza surrounded by columns with scroll-shaped details, known as Ionic columns: this is the Oval Forum of Jerash, 90 m long and 80 m wide. The cardo, the Roman city’s main street, begins here. Paved with stone, it runs north for 800 m. Its columns are Corinthian: their tops, called capitals, are carved with the leaves of the acanthus, a plant with large, deeply lobed leaves. Walk its full length, looking up as you go.

Measuring 22 m across, the nymphaeum of Jerash was a monumental 2nd-century fountain dedicated to the nymphs, deities of springs. A little farther on, the sanctuary of Artemis, goddess of the hunt, retains 11 of its 32 columns, nine of them 13 m tall. Their drums, the cylindrical blocks that form each column, are stacked without being fastened together. On windy days, some therefore sway very slightly. This flexibility also helps them withstand earthquakes. Climb the grand staircase to appreciate the temple’s size.

Next, climb to the South Theater of Jerash, built between 90 and 92 to hold around 5,000 spectators. In the center of the orchestra, the semicircular space at the foot of the seating, a stone marks a specific spot. From this stone, a normal speaking voice can be heard throughout the theater. Try it while a companion sits at the very top. Right next door, the 2nd-century Temple of Zeus retains walls 10 m high.

If you still have energy, continue to the northern part of Jerash. The North Theater, dating to 165, had just 800 seats. Nearby, the North Tetrapylon, a four-sided monument at the intersection of two streets, marks an ancient crossroads. The city had at least 14 churches, built between the 4th and 7th centuries. The Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, built around 533, retains a beautiful mosaic floor. Allow 1 hour for this area.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Jordan in 5 Days: Jerash, Ajloun, Umm Qais

visits.text: You explore Kerak Castle with a flashlight in hand, and that is part of its charm. The Crusaders, European knights who set out to conquer the Holy Land, began building it in the 1140s. In 1183, Sultan Saladin besieged it while a princely wedding was being celebrated inside. He agreed not to target the newlyweds’ room with his siege engines. The castle fell in 1188, after several months under siege. Allow two to three hours to explore its vaulted galleries, open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Set aside half an hour for the Al-Karak Archaeological Museum, housed since 2019 in an Ottoman building just outside the castle. Its galleries trace the region’s history from prehistoric times to the Islamic era. They will help you understand who built what. After the Crusaders, the Mamluks, sultans who ruled from Cairo, expanded the fortress. In 1263, Sultan Baybars added a tower at the northwest corner. Admission to both the museum and the castle is included in the Jordan Pass.

days_plan.itin_title: The King’s Highway in 6 Days: Madaba, Kerak, Dana, and Petra

visits.text: Little Petra, or Siq al-Barid, “the cold canyon,” lies 8 km north of Petra. The Nabataeans, the Arab caravan traders who built Petra, developed it in the 1st century to house visiting merchants. The Painted Biclinium is a banquet hall carved into the rock. Its paintings depict vines, birds, and small winged cupids picking grapes. It is the most complete known Nabataean painted scene. Admission is free, with no ticket required.

Seven thousand years before the Nabataeans, farmers were already living at Beidha, near Little Petra. This village dates to the Neolithic period, when humans began growing crops and raising animals. It was inhabited from about 7200 to 6500 BC. A fire devastated it around 6650 BC. Archaeologist Diana Kirkbride began excavating it in 1957. The site is part of the UNESCO-listed Petra property and is freely accessible: allow 30 minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: The King’s Highway in 6 Days: Madaba, Kerak, Dana, and Petra

visits.text: Set off early for Wadi Mujib, allowing for a day trip from Ma'in. The Siq Trail, nicknamed the “Grand Canyon of Jordan”, is a 3 km round-trip hike through water: you follow the river upstream between sandstone walls rising several dozen meters, with waist-deep water in places. The trail ends facing a waterfall. Allow 2 to 3 hours. Please note: restricted to visitors over 18, open only from April to October, closed in rainy weather. Bring a waterproof pouch for your phone and water shoes. Arrive as soon as it opens at 8 a.m. to avoid running into everyone on the way back.

After Mujib, head back up to the hot springs of Ma'in (Hammamat Ma'in). Waterfalls tumble down the wadi cliffs at temperatures that can reach 63 °C. The water is rich in sulfur, calcium and magnesium—Jordanians have bathed here for centuries, and tradition has it that King Herod the Great traveled from Jerusalem to treat his rheumatism. The natural pools at the foot of the waterfalls are accessible to everyone. After the cool canyon, the warmth of the springs makes a striking contrast.

On the route between Ma'in and the Dead Sea, detour to the Dead Sea Panoramic Complex. This viewpoint perched 400 meters above the shores offers a view down over the entire bluish expanse of the Dead Sea and the mountains opposite. A small museum traces the geological history and biodiversity of the region.

activities.text: Short hike in Wadi Zarqa Ma'in—a trail descending toward the waterfalls through a landscape of rock gorges and quasi-tropical vegetation, surprising in the middle of the desert.

days_plan.itin_title: Jordan Road Trip: Petra, Wadi Rum & the Dead Sea

places.name: Madaba

visits.text: Two fishing boats float on a mosaic Dead Sea on the floor of St. George’s Church in Madaba. This is the Madaba Map, laid in the 6th century. It remains the oldest surviving original map of the Holy Land and Jerusalem. It once contained more than two million tesserae, small cubes of colored stone, but only part of it survives. Look for Jerusalem in the center, then the fish in the Jordan River. Admission costs 1 Jordanian dinar (JD), and visits are not allowed during services.

Next, head to Madaba Archaeological Park, where a large shelter protects the mosaic floors of ancient houses and churches. In the Hall of Hippolytus, the central scene depicts the tragedy of Phaedra and Hippolytus, the Greek myth that inspired Racine’s play Phèdre. Outside, two sections of a Roman street that crossed the city have been uncovered. Admission is included in the Jordan Pass. Purchased online before departure, this pass covers the entry visa and more than 40 sites, including Petra.

Less well known than St. George’s, the Church of the Apostles in Madaba is worth a detour for a single mosaic. An inscription discovered in 1902 dates its construction to 578. In the center of the nave, the sea is depicted as a figure, a device known as personification. The mosaic artist signed his work with his name, Salamanios. The church stands at the southern entrance to the city, beside the King’s Highway. The archaeological park ticket also grants admission here.

Burned down at the end of the Byzantine period, this large residence in Madaba was never rebuilt. It is now known as the Burnt Palace. It dates from the late 6th or early 7th century. One of its rooms was decorated with mosaics. Pottery found on-site helps date its demise: the earthquake of 747 or 748 may have destroyed it for good. The site is included in the Jordan Pass; about twenty minutes is enough for a visit.

If you are not afraid of heights, climb the bell tower of the Shrine of the Beheading of St. John the Baptist. This early 20th-century Catholic church offers panoramic views of the entire city. The final stretch of the climb involves steep metal ladders between the bells and ropes. Beneath the church, vaulted cellars house a small museum. Here you can see a well about 3,000 years old, dug when the kingdom of Moab occupied this plateau, and still in use. Admission costs 1 JD and is not included in the Jordan Pass.

activities.text: You will land at Queen Alia Airport, south of Amman. Madaba is only 25 km away, so there is no need to go through the capital for your first night. Rent a car at the airport, as several sites along the King’s Highway, such as Shobak, are difficult to reach without a vehicle. If taking a taxi, negotiate the fare before getting in. If you arrive in the evening, go no farther than Madaba: France Diplomatie advises against driving at night.

days_plan.itin_title: The King’s Highway in 6 Days: Madaba, Kerak, Dana, and Petra

map_keywords: Madaba Map St George Church Madaba
Shrine of the Beheading of John the Baptist Madaba

visits.text: Mount Nebo, 10 km northwest of Madaba, is the summit from which Moses is said to have gazed upon the Promised Land before his death, according to the Bible. Monks lived here from the 4th to the 9th century. Their basilica, the Memorial of Moses, preserves Byzantine mosaics, including a peacock and a zebu, a humped ox. It reopened in October 2016 beneath a new protective roof. The Franciscans manage the site. Admission costs 3 JD and is not included in the Jordan Pass. Clothing must cover your shoulders and knees.

A metal sculpture, half cross and half serpent, stands against the sky on Mount Nebo. The work by Italian artist Gian Paolo Fantoni recalls two stories. The first is that of the bronze serpent Moses raised to heal the Hebrews who had been bitten by snakes. The second is the cross of Christ. The Jordan Valley stretches out before you: Jericho is usually visible, but Jerusalem can be seen only in very clear weather. The site closes its gates at 5 p.m.; arrive at least one hour beforehand, with a hat and water, as the terrace is exposed.

days_plan.itin_title: The King’s Highway in 6 Days: Madaba, Kerak, Dana, and Petra

visits.text: Pella, near the village of Tabaqat Fahl, lies almost at sea level, at the foot of the hills bordering the Jordan Valley. Near the spring stand the columns of the church in the civic complex, probably the former cathedral. It has three apses, the rounded recesses at the back of the chancel, and a grand staircase added in the 7th century. Beside it, a small Roman theater from the 1st century seated around 400 spectators. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the site.

In January 635, on the plain below Pella, a Muslim army annihilated the Byzantine forces. The city then surrendered under a treaty. To see this plain from above, climb to the 5th-century East Church, whose courtyard retains a small pool. Continue to the modern building with three arches known as the Resthouse, on the hill of Jabal Abu al-Khas. From there, the view stretches west across the Jordan Valley.

Finish your visit to Pella at the Canaanite temple, named after the peoples who lived here during the Bronze Age. Its stone blocks, dated to 1480 BCE, lie near a small mosque from the Mamluk period. Much later, according to the ancient historian Eusebius, Christians from Jerusalem took refuge in Pella. This was in the 1st century, during the Jewish revolt against Rome. Wear sturdy shoes to walk between the excavations.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Jordan in 5 Days: Jerash, Ajloun, Umm Qais

visits.text: Enter Petra as soon as it opens at 6 a.m. to walk through the Siq before the tour groups arrive. This natural gorge is just over 1.2 km long and narrows to 3 or 4 m in places. At the end, the Treasury, or al-Khazneh, comes into view, standing about 39 m tall and carved in the early 1st century. The bullet marks on the urn at the top were left by Bedouins who believed a pharaoh had hidden his treasure there. A one-day ticket costs 50 JD if you stay overnight in Jordan, or 90 JD otherwise. The cheapest Jordan Pass, at 70 JD, includes it.

The Street of Facades is lined with Nabataean tombs carved into the cliff, just beyond the Treasury. It leads to the theater, carved into the rock during the reign of the Nabataean king Aretas IV. It was cut into the foot of the High Place of Sacrifice, a Nabataean sanctuary perched on the mountain. The earthquake of 363 severely damaged the theater, along with much of the city. The main trail runs 3.9 km from the visitor center to Qasr al-Bint: allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 1 hour 45 minutes of walking, excluding stops.

In our view, the Royal Tombs offer the best panoramic view of central Petra. This group of facades includes the Urn Tomb, the Silk Tomb, the Corinthian Tomb, and the Palace Tomb. In 446, the Urn Tomb was converted into a church. A large courtyard stretches out in front of it, overlooking the heart of the city. Climb the steps to the Urn Tomb’s large courtyard for a view across the entire valley.

Petra is more than a city of the dead: on the valley floor, the Colonnaded Street recalls the city of the living. The Romans laid it out in the 2nd century. Nearby, the Great Temple is Petra’s largest building, covering 7,560 m², roughly the size of a soccer field. At the end of the street stands Qasr al-Bint, a temple marking the end of the main trail. Take your lunch break here: there are restaurants nearby, before the climb to the Monastery.

If you still have energy after lunch, climb to the Monastery, or Ad Deir. A path of nearly 800 steps leads there in about 40 minutes from the valley floor. Its facade measures 47 m high and 48 m wide, making it larger than the Treasury. Its purpose remains debated: a temple, a palace, or, later, a church during the Byzantine period. Set off by around 2 p.m. at the latest, carrying water, so you can descend before the site closes.

days_plan.itin_title: The King’s Highway in 6 Days: Madaba, Kerak, Dana, and Petra

visits.text: Qasr Kharana looks every bit like a fortress, but it is not one. Its narrow slits were not intended for archers: they ventilated the rooms, let in light, and kept dust down. This square building, measuring 35 m on each side, has around sixty rooms on two levels surrounding a courtyard that collected rainwater. One inscription dates to 710. Researchers believe the building served as a meeting place for the chiefs of Bedouin tribes, the desert nomads. Open from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. October through April, and until 6 p.m. May through September.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Jordan in 5 Days: Jerash, Ajloun, Umm Qais

visits.text: Although more ruined than Kerak, Shobak Castle makes an even stronger impression from a distance, standing alone on its hill. It was the first castle built by the Crusaders east of the Jordan River. King Baldwin I of Jerusalem founded it in 1115 and named it Montréal, the “royal mountain.” Saladin did not capture it until May 1189, after nearly two years under siege. Look for the inscriptions in Arabic calligraphy left by the Mamluks on the towers. Near the entrance, a staircase of 375 steps descends to the old spring: do not enter, as visitors have been seriously injured there.

The north side of Shobak Castle reveals its more recent history: the site remained inhabited until the 1950s. You will see abandoned Ottoman houses and the old village school, with its three arched entrances. Farther on, an Ayyubid palace still has its reception hall and baths. The Ayyubids were Saladin’s dynasty. Admission costs 1 JD or is included in the Jordan Pass. Local guides offer their services at the gate for about ten dinars.

days_plan.itin_title: The King’s Highway in 6 Days: Madaba, Kerak, Dana, and Petra

places.name: Umm Ar Rasas

visits.text: In 785, mosaic artists depicted cities of the Holy Land and Egypt on the floor of St. Stephen’s Church in Umm ar-Rasas. Each city is labeled with its name in Greek: Jerusalem, Gaza, and Alexandria, as well as Madaba and Kerak, two stops on this trip. Later, some figures were deliberately obscured. Their tesserae were removed, then relaid out of order. The site has been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 2004. It is included in the Jordan Pass and is open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Kastron Mefaa, the ancient name of Umm ar-Rasas, originally referred to a fortified Roman military camp. From the 5th century onward, a town developed within its walls. UNESCO lists sixteen churches here, and much of the site has never been excavated. After seeing the mosaic, walk along the enclosure walls to appreciate the size of the former camp. The ground is uneven, so sturdy shoes are useful.

The most unusual monument at Umm ar-Rasas stands about 1.6 km north of the ruins: a stone tower 14 m tall. It rises in the center of a courtyard beside a small church. Stylites lived here, monks who isolated themselves atop a column or tower to pray. The room at the top served as their living quarters. Save it for the end of your visit: allow about twenty minutes to walk there from the enclosure.

map_keywords: Church of St Stephen Umm ar-Rasas

visits.text: Black stone underfoot, black stone in the seating tiers: the West Theater at Umm Qais is built entirely of basalt, a dark volcanic rock. It held around 3,000 spectators, with local dignitaries occupying high-backed seats. This is where the headless statue of Tyche, the city’s goddess of fortune, was found; it is now in the site museum. Come early in the morning, while the stone is still cool.

Next, head to the rock-cut basilica terrace at Umm Qais. A Byzantine church from the 5th–6th centuries stood here, its octagonal layout surrounded by black basalt columns. The panorama takes in Lake Tiberias, also called the Sea of Galilee, the Golan Heights, and the Yarmouk Gorge. On clear days, Mount Hermon is also visible. The border is close: do not photograph military personnel or checkpoints.

Roman ruins below, Ottoman houses above: at Umm Qais, the village of black basalt and white limestone reused stones from ancient Gadara. It dates to the Ottoman period, when the Turkish empire ruled the region. Now abandoned, it is open to explore freely. The former governor’s residence, Beit Rousan, houses the museum, with mosaics, carved sarcophagi (stone coffins), and the Tyche statue from the theater. Farther on, the decumanus, a broad paved street running east–west, still bears wheel ruts. Admission to the site includes the museum.

activities.text: The most beautiful time at Umm Qais is the evening, after the day-trippers from Amman have left. Staying overnight lets you enjoy twilight and the cool of the morning, two moments you miss on a day trip. Settle at the edge of the basilica terrace and watch the light fade over the Jordan Valley. If possible, avoid Friday, when families and groups of young people come for outings.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Jordan in 5 Days: Jerash, Ajloun, Umm Qais

visits.text: South of Dhiban, the plateau ends abruptly: the Wadi Mujib canyon opens before you, more than 500 m deep and 4 km wide at the top. In the Bible, this river is called the Arnon; it marked the northern border of the kingdom of Moab. The Mesha Stele, a stone inscribed around 850 BC, was found in Dhiban, the former capital of Moab. On it, King Mesha recounts how he freed Moab from Israel’s rule. It is displayed at the Louvre. Stop at the small overlook just beyond the canyon rim.

You will then follow switchbacks down to the Mujib Dam at the bottom of the canyon. Completed in 2004, it holds up to 35 million m³ of water, equivalent to about 14,000 Olympic swimming pools. The King’s Highway crosses its crest. At the bottom of the valley, the air is noticeably warmer than on the plateau. During thunderstorms, do not linger: a wadi is an often-dry valley where floodwaters can rise very quickly. The climb back up toward Kerak then follows a series of sharp bends.

days_plan.itin_title: The King’s Highway in 6 Days: Madaba, Kerak, Dana, and Petra

visits.text: Enter Petra through the Siq, a 1.2-km canyon whose multicolored sandstone walls narrow to 3–4 meters wide. After a final turn, Al-Khazneh (the Treasury) appears: a 39-meter-high by 25-meter-wide façade carved from rose sandstone, probably a tomb for the Nabataean king Aretas IV (1st century BCE). The Bedouins believed an urn at the top held treasure and shot at it—the bullet impacts are still visible on this 3.5-meter urn carved from solid rock. Be there as soon as it opens, around 6–7 a.m., when the sun illuminates the façade and the stone turns bright pink—and especially before the groups arrive.

Continue beyond the Treasury to the Street of Facades, where about forty rock-cut tombs line the cliff face, then to the Nabataean theater carved from the sandstone, capable of seating around 3,000 spectators. Opposite, on the east cliff, the Royal Tombs merit the climb: the Urn Tomb offers a view down over the entire Petra valley. Estimates suggest only 10% of the site has been excavated to date.

Push on to the High Place of Sacrifice, accessible by a steep but short trail (20–30 min ascent). At the summit, a Nabataean altar carved from rock and a 360° view across Petra's mountains. The descent via Wadi Farasa lets you see less-frequented tombs and façades barely weathered by time.

End the day with the Colonnaded Street and Qasr al-Bint, one of Petra's rare built structures (not carved from rock)—probably a temple dedicated to the Nabataeans' principal deity. This is where French CNRS archaeologists conducted excavations that highlighted the city's urban character.

activities.text: Petra by Night: the Treasury lit by 1,500 candles, accompanied by Bedouin music and sage tea. Offered from Sunday to Thursday—inquire at the visitor center.

days_plan.itin_title: Jordan Road Trip: Petra, Wadi Rum & the Dead Sea
The King’s Highway in 6 Days: Madaba, Kerak, Dana, and Petra

places.name: Wadi Rum

visits.text: Second day at Petra—head for the Monastery (Ad Deir). Climb the 800 steps from the central basin: the ascent takes 45 minutes to an hour, but at the summit you discover a façade 47 meters wide by 48 meters high, even more massive than the Treasury but in a far wilder setting. Bedouins run a small tea house directly opposite—take a break with a view. Descend by the same path or explore the trail to the viewpoint overlooking the valley.

On the way down toward the exit, stop at the Obelisk Tomb at the Siq entrance. It consists of two monuments, one above the other: above, four obelisks representing the deceased, and below, a triclinium (funerary banquet hall). If you have a bit of time, make a detour to Little Petra (Siq al-Barid), 10 minutes by car north of Wadi Musa—a mini-canyon with Nabataean façades and far fewer people.

In the afternoon, take the road to Wadi Rum (~1.5 hours from Wadi Musa). At the visitor center, board a 4x4 driven by a Bedouin guide. Wadi Rum, UNESCO-listed since 2011 (mixed natural and cultural site), covers 74,000 hectares of red sand and sandstone towers sometimes exceeding 1,800 meters. The circuit passes through Khazali Canyon, where 12,000-year-old petroglyphs show hunting scenes, then by the Um Fruth arch, easily accessible on foot. The desert has served as backdrop for Lawrence of Arabia, The Martian and other films.

Finish the 4x4 tour with a stop at sunset on a red dune in the south. When the low-angle light strikes the sandstone monoliths, the palette shifts from golden yellow to deep red in a few minutes. Complete silence, not a car, not a sound—it's the most powerful moment of the day.

activities.text: Night at a Bedouin camp in Wadi Rum—traditional tents or sleeping under the stars depending on the season. The zarb dinner (chicken and vegetables cooked in a sealed pit under the sand) is followed by sweet tea around the fire. Far from any light pollution, the night sky is spectacular—you'll make out the Milky Way with the naked eye.
